title: The serpent who came to teach
hook: a tiny snake falls into a praying woman's hands and grows up to teach yoga's eight limbs
carry: eight limbs, and ethics come first

segments.voice: Yesterday: aviplava, unwavering, and your line, viveka: telling the self from what it sees. Virochana stopped at the reflection, Indra kept going back. Today, the teacher behind this book.
screen: `VIVEKA: TELLING THE SELF FROM WHAT IT SEES — INDRA GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: A woman named Gonika stands at a river at sunrise, offering water to the sun from her cupped hands. For years she has prayed for someone to pass her learning on to. As she lifts her hands, something tiny drops into them: a little snake. It becomes a child. A traditional story, still told in yoga schools, says this was Shesha, the great serpent Vishnu rests on, come down to teach. Fallen, pata, into folded hands, anjali. Patanjali.
screen: `A WOMAN OFFERS WATER TO THE SUN.` → `A TINY SNAKE FALLS INTO HER HANDS.` → `PATA, ANJALI.`

segments.voice: That's why statues of Patanjali often show a sage whose lower body is a serpent's coil, with hoods spread over his head. Many yoga classes still open with an old verse that bows to him with folded hands, the sage who cleared the mind with yoga, speech with grammar and the body with medicine. Many teachers read the story as a picture of how Hindus hold this book: yoga as a gift that came down to clean a person all the way through. So what did he teach? Sutra 2.29 lists the eight limbs, ashtanga. Ashta, eight; anga, limb. Yama, the restraints: how you treat others. Niyama, the observances: how you keep yourself. Asana, the seat. Pranayama, the breath. Pratyahara, the senses drawing back. Dharana, concentration. Dhyana, meditation. Samadhi, absorption. Listen to the direction. It starts with other people and moves inward, until only the object shines. Teachers read the shape two ways: a ladder, ethics first and then body and mind; or limbs, which grow together, like a child's arms and legs. Either way, the proportion is plain. Ethics first, twice. Posture, one word out of eight. So when a studio timetable says Ashtanga, six p.m., bring water, that class is a modern tradition of its own. The word behind it is older, and in the sutra it begins with how you treat the people in the room.
screen: `A SAGE WITH A SERPENT'S COIL.` · `ASHTA: EIGHT. ANGA: LIMB.` · `FROM OTHERS, INWARD TO ABSORPTION.` · `ONE POSTURE OUT OF EIGHT.` · then, large: `ETHICS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Walk the eight in miniature: a moment of goodwill toward someone, contentment with this exact moment, a steady and easy seat, a slightly longer breath, sounds and sights left in the background. Then rest your attention on one point, maybe the breath at the nostrils, let it flow without breaks, and if the point fills everything, let it. If it doesn't, that's normal.
Ashtanga. The eight parts of yoga in sutra 2.29, from how you treat others all the way in to absorption.
Your line: eight limbs, and ethics come first. The serpent came down to teach all eight, not just the poses. Day four hundred fifty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Many yoga classes open with a chant bowing to Patanjali, often pictured with a serpent's coil and hoods; classical teaching presents the eight limbs of 2.29 as the framework of the whole practice, starting with the restraints and observances.

original.note: Sanskrit aṣṭāṅga: aṣṭa (eight) plus aṅga (limb, part); the eight limbs of yoga in 2.29.

trapdoor: what you thought: ashtanga is a sweaty yoga class.
what it means: eight limbs of one practice, moving from ethics to absorption, with posture one part of eight.
what a scholar hears: ashta plus anga in 2.29; a later traditional story makes Patanjali an incarnation of Shesha, which is why he's shown with a serpent's hoods.

Patanjali.meaning: the sage credited with the Yoga Sutras

Shesha.meaning: the great serpent Vishnu rests on

Ashtanga.meaning: eight limbs: ashta, eight, and anga, limb

niyama.meaning: the observances: how you treat yourself

sources.ref: Traditional story of Patanjali's birth (Gonika; Shesha falls into her cupped hands), told in later tradition and yoga schools
Traditional invocation to Patanjali (yoga for the mind, grammar for speech, medicine for the body)

notes: Ashtanga Vinyasa as a modern style 'built in the twentieth century in Mysore' (Krishnamacharya, K. Pattabhi Jois): kept unnamed and general; confirm the framing is fair.
Sequential versus simultaneous readings of the limbs: presented as two long-standing readings without attribution; a Keeper may wish to name commentators.
Pranayama is described as 'working with the breath'; some will argue two limbs (asana, pranayama) involve the body. The 'one posture' claim is literal.
